name: Storyboarding and Pre-visualization
title: Storyboarding and Pre-visualization
answer: AI storyboarding and pre-visualization covers the use of generative image and video models to turn scripts, shot lists, and director's notes into rough visual sequences before production. It includes character blocking, camera framing, lighting references, and timing studies for scenes. The output is not final footage but a working document that helps cinematographers, production designers, and editors align on visual intent. This practice sits between traditional hand-drawn boards and full animatics, and it is increasingly used for pitches, location scouting, and VFX planning.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on cloud GPU services or local workstations with enough VRAM to run diffusion-based image models and early video generation models. A typical pipeline stores prompts, seed values, and generated frames in a versioned asset manager so that a board can be regenerated consistently. Because pre-visualization often requires many iterations per shot, teams use batch rendering and low-resolution previews first, then upscale only the frames that survive review. Some studios keep these tools behind a firewall to protect unreleased scripts and actor likenesses.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is iterative prompting and image-to-image refinement. An artist or assistant starts with a written shot description, generates a rough frame, then adjusts composition, lens feel, and lighting through prompt changes, inpainting, or control layers such as depth and pose maps. For motion, short video clips are generated from keyframes to test camera moves and blocking. The result is a board or animatic that can be edited into a timeline with temporary dialogue and sound, giving the team a shared sense of pace before any camera is rented.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on who owns the generated frames, whether training data included copyrighted films or photographs, and whether an actor's face or a distinctive set design can be reproduced without clearance. Studios often require that pre-visualization outputs be treated as internal working materials, not for public release, to reduce infringement exposure. Contracts with vendors should state that generated boards are work for hire and that no third-party model may retain or train on the studio's prompts or frames. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, which is a reminder that this area is still unsettled.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Pre-visualization is moving toward real-time, director-driven tools where a shot can be blocked in a virtual space and rendered as a rough video in seconds. As video models improve, boards will become short animatics with consistent characters and camera physics, reducing the gap between pre-vis and final footage. The likely outcome is a tighter loop between script, storyboard, and on-set reference, with cinematographers using generated frames to pre-light scenes and VFX supervisors using them to plan plates. The site's tracking of 1000 video models suggests the tooling will keep diversifying, but the craft will remain in the hands of people who know how to read a shot.
